Boyko Borisov Labels President Radev the New Orban and Discusses Potential Government Coalitions
Boyko Borisov, leader of the GERB party, labeled President Rumen Radev as the “new Viktor Orban” during a campaign closing event in Samokov on April 15, 2026. Borisov alleged secret diplomatic meetings and warned against increasing national debt, signaling a sharp escalation in the battle for Bulgaria’s political future.
The air in Samokov was thick with political tension as approximately 3,000 supporters gathered at the Arena Samokov. This wasn’t just a campaign wrap-up; it was a strategic strike. Borisov used the platform to draw a provocative parallel between the Bulgarian presidency and the controversial leadership style of Hungary’s Viktor Orban. By doing so, he shifted the narrative from simple policy disagreements to a fundamental clash over the nature of Bulgarian democracy.
This level of volatility creates a precarious environment for the private sector. When the highest levels of government are locked in a war of words regarding “oligarchs” and “secret diplomacy,” market stability wavers. For many business owners, this is the moment where they stop relying on political promises and start engaging corporate legal experts to protect their assets from the whims of shifting administrations.
The “Orban” Label: A Calculated Comparison
Borisov’s choice of words was not accidental. He explicitly linked Rumen Radev to Viktor Orban, but with a twist of timing. He noted that Orban had recently lost the elections in Hungary, a leader with whom Borisov previously maintained warm relations. Borisov was careful to distinguish himself from the Hungarian leader, describing Orban as an “anti-communist” and a “friend,” while asserting that the differences between their approaches are “huge.”
The core of the accusation is that Radev is adopting a similar brand of illiberalism. By framing Radev as the “new Orban,” Borisov is warning the electorate that the presidency is moving toward a model of centralized power that bypasses traditional democratic norms.
We see a high-stakes game of perception.
Borisov further amplified this by contrasting his own coalition’s funding with that of his rivals. He asserted that GERB-SDS does not have “oligarch donors,” unlike other “progressive parties.” This attack on the financial integrity of his opponents is designed to frame GERB as the only transparent option in a field of puppets.
Shadow Diplomacy and the Zhelyazkov Cabinet
The most explosive claim made in Samokov involves a breach of diplomatic protocol. Borisov alleged that during the tenure of the Zhelyazkov cabinet, Viktor Orban’s foreign minister conducted a secret visit to President Rumen Radev. According to Borisov, this meeting happened without the knowledge or notification of the Bulgarian government in Sofia.
The source of this information, Borisov claims, was Georgi Georgiev, who served as the Foreign Minister appointed by GERB at the time. The implication is clear: Radev was conducting a parallel foreign policy, operating in the shadows of the official state apparatus.
“We now have the new Viktor Orban in the person of Rumen Radev, and it is not a coincidence that Orban’s foreign minister came secretly to Radev while he was president.”
This allegation of “secret diplomacy” suggests a fragmentation of state authority. When the presidency and the foreign ministry are not in sync, international partners are left wondering who actually speaks for the country. For firms operating on the international stage, this ambiguity is a red flag. Navigating these diplomatic fractures often requires the guidance of international business consultants who can read the unspoken signals of the Bulgarian state.
The Economic Battleground: Debt and Taxes
Beyond the personality clashes, Borisov pivoted to the ledger. He declared a firm stance against any policies that would increase the national debt. The rhetoric was blunt: he does not want a party that condemns children and youth to pay off “foreign debts.”
Instead, Borisov is positioning GERB as the champion of economic growth, insisting on measures that support business and investment. This is a direct challenge to the perceived fiscal direction of his opponents.
The tension here is between two different visions of the state. One side views government spending as a tool for immediate social stability, while Borisov argues that such spending, if funded by debt, is a generational betrayal.
In a climate where tax hikes are frequently debated, the uncertainty is stifling. Local enterprises are increasingly seeking strategic financial planners to hedge against the possibility of sudden fiscal shifts that could erode their margins overnight.
The Looming Coalition: PP-DB and the Peevski Factor
The political map Borisov painted in Samokov extends beyond the presidency. He raised the possibility of a government formed by the “Continue the Change-Democratic Bulgaria” (PP-DB) alliance and “Progressive Bulgaria.” However, he added a cynical layer to this potential partnership, suggesting that Delyan Peevski might be providing “slight support” from the sidelines.
This suggests a complex web of dependencies. Borisov is attempting to link the “progressive” image of PP-DB to the controversial influence of Peevski, effectively poisoning the well for any potential coalition they might form.
The current political landscape can be summarized by these competing interests:
- GERB-SDS: Positioning themselves as the anti-debt, anti-oligarch alternative with a focus on business growth.
- Rumen Radev: Accused of practicing “Orban-style” politics and secret diplomacy.
- PP-DB / Progressive Bulgaria: Attempting to navigate a path toward government while facing accusations of secret backing by powerful intermediaries.
The volatility of this arrangement means that municipal laws and regional infrastructure projects could be stalled indefinitely. If the central government remains in a state of flux, the flow of funds to the provinces—including places like Samokov—becomes unpredictable.
Bulgaria is currently navigating a period of profound institutional instability. The clash between Borisov and Radev is not merely a personal feud; it is a struggle over the very blueprint of the Bulgarian state. Whether the country moves toward a more centralized, “Orban-esque” model or maintains its current trajectory depends on the outcome of these political maneuvers.
